TRANSCRIPT OF PROCEEDINGS
THE HON CATHERINE HOLMES AC SC, Commissioner
THE ROYAL COMMISSION INTO THE ROBODEBT SCHEME
WEDNESDAY, 22 FEBRUARY 2023 AT 10:01 AM (AEST)
DAY 34
MR ANGUS SCOTT KC, Senior Counsel Assisting
MS SALWA MARSH, Counsel Assisting
MS DOMINIQUE HOGAN-DORAN SC, for the Commonwealth
MR ALEXANDER VIAL, for the Commonwealth

COMMISSIONER: So I see, Mr Scott, you are appearing with Ms Marsh and, Ms Hogan-Doran,
with Mr Vial?
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Commissioner, before we commence today's evidence, can I tender the exhibits
in the list for today's proceedings?
COMMISSIONER: Yes. So 5353 to 5663; is that right?
MR SCOTT: It should be to five - yes, that's right, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. The exhibits as described on the list are admitted with those
numbers. Yes.
<EXHIBITS 5353 TO 5663 TENDERED AS PER THE EXHIBIT LIST
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. I call Matthew Roser.
COMMISSIONER: Mr Roser, will you take an oath or an affirmation?
MR ROSER: The oath, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Okay. If you would stand, it will be administered.
<MATTHEW RICHARD WANDSWORTH ROSER, SWORN
<EXAMINATION BY MR SCOTT
COMMISSIONER: Thanks. Take a seat. Yes, Mr Scott.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Mr Roser, could you please state your full name?
MR ROSER: Matthew Richard Wandsworth Roser, R-o-s-e-r.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. You were provided a Notice to Give Information in Writing and
Produce Documents dated the 18th of October 2022?
MR ROSER: That's correct.
MR SCOTT: You produced a Statement in response to that Notice dated the 21st of October
2022?

MR SCOTT: You produced a Supplementary Statement dated the 20th of February 2023?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Are the contents of your Statements true and correct to the best of your
knowledge and belief?
MR ROSER: They are.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Commissioner, could I just one raise one matter, I thought I had raised
with my learned friend, as to a correction to paragraph 76.
MR SCOTT: Yes, I was going to raise that.
MS HOGAN-DORAN: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Now, you've got some folders there in front of you, Mr Roser?
MR ROSER: I do.
MR SCOTT: Can you just identify what those folders are?
MR ROSER: One is marked Robodebt Royal Commission Hearing Block 4 with the names Tim
Ffrench and Matthew Roser, Witness Bundle Volume 2 of 2. One is the same except it is
Witness Bundle Volume 1 of 2. The third folder is Hearing Block 3 AAT Bundle, Witness
Bundle Volume 1 of 1. And the fourth one is marked Hearing Block 4, Matthew Roser
Supplementary Witness Bundle.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Is it the case, as mentioned by my learned friend, you have a
correction to make to paragraph 76 of your Statement?
MR ROSER: I do.
MR SCOTT: Which Statement is that?
MR ROSER: The first Statement of October.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what's that correction?
MR ROSER: In paragraph 76, there's an additional superfluous "not" about three lines from
the bottom.
MR SCOTT: Perhaps if we can have that up on the screen so we can see what you are talking
about.

MR ROSER: Yes. Thank you. It's the "not" before the word "wrong" which should, obviously,
be removed.
MR SCOTT: Yes. Thank you. I will just ask that that be brought up on the screen. That's on
page 14. If we call out paragraph 76.
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: It's the fourth sentence, is it?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes, it is.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And there's a "not". Which "not" should be - - -
MR ROSER: Three lines from the bottom where the sentence ends "the original letter was
not wrong" should read "the original letter was wrong".
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Subject to that clarification, is that Statement true and correct to the
best of your knowledge and belief?
MR ROSER: It is.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Now, you were employed by DHS as a General Counsel, DHS being the
Department of Human Services, between 22 May 2017 and 15 November 2019?
MR ROSER: I was.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And what team did you - were you responsible for as General Counsel in
that capacity?
MR ROSER: Initially on joining the Department, I was responsible for a branch that covered
FOI, subpoenas and litigation. There was a restructure, I think, late in about 2018 where I
became responsible for a branch that traded out FOI and traded in what we call information
release, which was an administrative release scheme to allow customers to speedily obtain
their own Departmental documents.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And during your time as General Counsel during the period we have
described, where were you geographically located while at work?
MR ROSER: In Forrest - in the Doris Blackburn Building in Forrest, Canberra.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Thank you. Was there a person in that team called - by the way, was that
team known also as the FOIL team?
MR ROSER: Initially, when it was FOI and Litigation.

MR ROSER: There was in the litigation team in Hobart, yes.
MR SCOTT: So he was geographically located in Hobart?
MR ROSER: Yes, he was.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Did he spend much time working in Canberra?
MR ROSER: None at all in my time there. He may have before my time.
MR SCOTT: And is this right: until - sorry, from 22nd May 2017 until January 2019, you
reported to Annette Musolino?
MR ROSER: Yes. As Chief Counsel, yes.
MR SCOTT: And then thereafter, Tim Ffrench?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Prior to holding this General Counsel role in the Department of
Human Services, were you a partner at Mills Oakley?
MR ROSER: Yes, I was.
MR SCOTT: What area of law did you practice in?
MR ROSER: General litigation, specifically Commonwealth focused.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And would that include litigation in the field of administrative law?
MR ROSER: It would, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And would you therefore have had familiarity with the principle of
administrative law that administrative decisions are generally required to be based on
evidence?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And that an administrative decision that's not based on evidence is potentially
invalid?
MR ROSER: As a general proposition, yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. Now, in your role as General Counsel in the FOIL team, is this
right - sorry, I withdraw that. Is this right: was the FOIL team a team that had responsibility

MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And those advices, were they in a standard form known as an AFAR?
MR ROSER: They were.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And would those Tier 1 decisions include decisions regarding matters
under the Robodebt Scheme?
MR ROSER: They would.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So would this be right: during your time as General Counsel, you became
aware of how debts were calculated and raised under the Robodebt Scheme?
MR ROSER: I did, after the commencement of the litigation by Ms Masterton.
MR SCOTT: So you didn't become aware of how the debts were calculated and raised under
that Scheme before that?
MR ROSER: No.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And the litigation commenced by Ms Masterton was in February 2019?
MR ROSER: Yes, it was.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So can you explain how, as General Counsel responsible for the team that
provided advice on Tier 1 AAT decisions regarding the Robodebt Scheme, you didn't become
aware of how debts were calculated and raised under that Scheme prior to February 2019?
MR ROSER: It had never become an issue for me as General Counsel. In terms of the way the
litigation was handled in the Department, the AAT Tier 1 or Social Security Appeals Tribunal
was basically administered by another branch, a non-legal branch. There was a bundle of
paperwork put forward on behalf of the Commonwealth, for want of a better term.
MR SCOTT: Sorry, I will just stop you there. When you say, "a bundle of paperwork put
forward", what are you referring to?
MR ROSER: It was not my area. It was done by another branch, so I don't know what was in
the bundle of paperwork. I just understand that paperwork was provided to AAT Tier 1.
MR SCOTT: Right.
COMMISSIONER: Are you talking about what we would call the T docs?
MR ROSER: They would be a form of T docs, yes. Yes, Commissioner.

MR SCOTT: Okay. Sorry I interrupted you, Mr Roser. I just wanted to clarify that.
MR ROSER: No, no, no. Thank you. And so those matters in AAT1 would have numbered
possibly somewhere around 10 or 12 thousand a year. Decisions that were adverse to the
Commonwealth, which was a relatively, as I understand it, small percentage would then be
assessed with an AFAR as to whether an appeal would be taken to AAT2. At the end of AAT2,
if there were decisions adverse to what you might call the Commonwealth interests, then
another AFAR would be done as to whether the matter would be taken on further appeal,
usually to either the Federal Court or the Federal Circuit Court.
But that was a system that was - because even the AAT2 numbers that were dealt with by my
litigation team and also by external providers instructed by my team, they numbered
probably two and a half to three to maybe three and a half thousand a year. That was not
something that I was dipping into on a day-to-day basis. That was something that was done
by my expert litigators because they were precisely that, subject matter experts in the whole
panoply of the litigation that they were running or was being run by external legal service
providers.
MR SCOTT: Did they - did you have a system whereby you would cause your litigators to
inform you of significant legal issues that were arising in AAT Tier 1 matters?
MR ROSER: Not specifically limited to AAT Tier 1, but it was always clear that if there were
significant issues that needed to be elevated in any aspect of litigation, then that should be
done because I would then need to make an assessment as to what, if anything, could and
should be done and whether further escalation was required. So that was effectively a kind
of a standing known, for want of a better term.
MR SCOTT: What about a regular meeting?
MR ROSER: We met regularly every week. The - not the entire team. I met with the Deputy
General Counsel, who were EL2 - Executive Level 2 lawyers, who were basically heading up
the litigation teams in various geographic locations. We would meet once a week with a
formal agenda, which included any sort of items of interest or new urgent issues that needed
to be raised as the group. The entire litigation team, I think we only met as an entire national
team maybe once a month.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So those once-a-week meetings with your Deputy General Counsels, was it
usual practice for significant legal issues to be raised and discussed?
MR ROSER: It did occur, but generally litigation was a relatively quiet component of my
branch, particularly in the early days when I was responsible also for FOI. Most of the
litigation issues that were discussed revolved around staffing and resourcing and those more
administrative type of issues.
MR SCOTT: Alright. So is it your evidence that at no stage during any of those meetings that
you recall was the issue of the lawfulness of averaging as it was used in the Robodebt

MR ROSER: I don't have any recollection of it being raised until the time of Ms Masterton's
claim, when, of course, we did then discuss it in subsequent meetings.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Were you aware that there was some substantial media publicity around
the Robodebt Scheme in early 2017?
MR ROSER: I am aware now. I actually wasn't aware at the time.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So you weren't aware of any adverse media commentary about the
lawfulness of averaging before Ms Masterton's litigation in February 2019?
MR ROSER: I became aware of media reporting and what you might call publicity, for want of
a better term, before the commencement of Ms Masterton's litigation, but not in 2017. I
suspect, from memory, it was some time around the middle or towards the end of 2018. I
can't be certain, I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall an article by Terry Carney in 2018 about the lawfulness of
averaging?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And when did you become aware of that article?
MR ROSER: I'm afraid I can't recall whether - it was after it was initially published. It was
brought to my attention by someone, but I couldn't - I'm afraid I can't recall at what point.
COMMISSIONER: Did you take an interest in the cases he had decided in the AAT on the
issue? Because having read the article, you must have known he had been an AAT member.
MR ROSER: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: So did it occur to you to have a look at what he had actually decided?
MR ROSER: It did. I didn't go back and look at AAT decisions, but I did read the articles and
there was - I was conscious of increasing media reporting.
COMMISSIONER: But didn't you put two and two together and think, "Well, there must have
been decisions about this and what did we do with them"?
MR ROSER: No, I didn't take that step, Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: Did it occur to you?
MR ROSER: Not that I recall.

MR SCOTT: Can the witness please be shown - and, Mr Roser, it should be behind your tab 23
of the AAT bundle - Exhibit 3482, Doc ID CTH.3761.0001.0223.
MR ROSER: Sorry, tab 24?
MR SCOTT: 23.
MR ROSER: 23. Yes, yes.
MR SCOTT: Do you have that?
MR ROSER: I have it.
MR SCOTT: Now, have you had an opportunity to look at this decision in preparation for your
evidence today?
MR ROSER: I can't say because the name I - I mainly went by the applicant, which is redacted.
So I'm not sure by the date of Wednesday, the 8 of March, whether it is - I'm assuming - I'm
speculating that it is either the [REDACTED] or the [REDACTED] decision.
MR SCOTT: We just can't mention the name.
MR ROSER: Sorry.
COMMISSIONER: Write it on a bit of paper for him, for goodness sake.
MR SCOTT: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: There must be a way of communicating this.
MR ROSER: Thank you. I have that decision.
MR SCOTT: Now, having read that decision - and I appreciate this is prior to you becoming
General Counsel in the Department. But having read that decision, do you accept that the
effect of it is that the use of averaging as it was being applied in the Robodebt Scheme to
calculate debts and raise those debts was unlawful?
MR ROSER: I - I accept that that was this decision, yes. Yes, absolutely.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And that the tribunal had specifically directed that no debt or debt
component is able to be founded on extrapolations from Australian Tax Office records?
MR ROSER: Yes.

MR SCOTT: And that it had specifically directed that:
The earnings components of any recalculated debt as may be raised must be based on and
confined to any fortnightly salary records obtainable in the exercise of statutory powers to do
so.
Do you see that?
MR ROSER: I recall that, yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: And are you aware that that decision was not appealed?
MR ROSER: I am aware, yes.
MR SCOTT: And that those directions were thereby binding on the Department of Human
Services?
MR ROSER: Yes, that's correct.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Now, could the witness please be shown - I will just get the tab number
for you in that same bundle, Mr Sparkes, but it is Exhibit 3485, CTH.0010.0002.0234_R. It
should be a chain of emails. It's your tab 26.
MR ROSER: Thank you. Yes, I have it.
MR SCOTT: You have that? Have you had an opportunity to review this chain of emails in
your preparation for your evidence today?
MR ROSER: Yes, I have.
MR SCOTT: Okay. If we go to the last email in the chain. Do you see that's dated the 30th of
May 2017?
MR ROSER: Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: That, of course, is just over a week after you've started as General Counsel for
the FOIL team?
MR ROSER: Yes. Correct.
MR SCOTT: The author of the email says that she's:
...doing an implementation where the AAT has requested we obtain income verification from
four employers in order to recalculate the debt.
Do you see that?

MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And having reviewed this email chain prior to your evidence today, do you accept
that this relates to the AAT decision that we just discussed shortly?
MR ROSER: Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And you see that the author of the email identifies a difficulty with
obtaining information from one of the employers because they are now out of business, and
that the income from that employer formed the bulk of the debt that was in issue?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: And the question is:
Please advise what information is to be used in the recalculation. The AAT indicates we
cannot use the ATO data, however there was a significant discrepancy.
Do you see that?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes, I do.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And then if we go to the next email in the chain on the second-last page
from Mr Baril. And Mr Baril was in your team, wasn't he, at the time?
MR ROSER: I - I'm afraid I have no idea.
MR SCOTT: Well, the bottom - - -
MR ROSER: I mean, I assume he is, yes. Yes. But I didn't have any actual knowledge of that at
the time. But his signature block indicates - yes. Sorry.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So you don't recall him being in your team?
MR ROSER: No.
MR SCOTT: Okay.
MR ROSER: It's a large team, I'm afraid, but I didn't recall every secondee.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Well, in any event, you can see that he - his email identifies the issue that
the author of the previous email identified about calculating the debt?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: And asked the question as to what is to be done, in effect?

MR ROSER: Yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: And if we go to the next email in the chain that starts on the bottom of the
previous page and call the full email out, please. Now, that's an email from Mr Sparkes dated
the 30th of May 2017?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: You have read that email in preparation for today's evidence?
MR ROSER: Yes, I have.
MR SCOTT: Do you agree that the effect of what Mr Sparkes advises is that the recalculated
debt could be recalculated using averaging contrary to the specific direction of the AAT?
MR ROSER: That is what his email says, yes.
MR SCOTT: Alright. And just to complete the sequence, if we go to the first page, call out the
email on the bottom of the page - the bottom of the first page, the last four digits 0234.
MR ROSER: Yes, yes.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Do you agree with me that it would appear that the Department thereby
recalculated the debt in accordance with Mr Sparkes' advice?
MR ROSER: That's how it appears to me, yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Now, do you understand that actions taken by officers of the
Commonwealth contrary to directions of the AAT may well be a contempt of court - sorry,
contempt of the tribunal, I beg your pardon?
MR ROSER: It - it is certainly possible, yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: Okay. And can you explain how a lawyer in your team gave advice to members of
the Department to act contrary to a direction of the AAT?
MR ROSER: I can't explain what motivated Mr Sparkes on that occasion, I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: Is that consistent with the standards of conduct you expected of your lawyers
within your team at the time?
MR ROSER: No.
MR SCOTT: And how did - how did you set the ethical standards for lawyers within your team
at the time?

MR ROSER: It's not something I specifically focused on. They, as I said, are very experienced
litigators. The Deputy General Counsels and the EL2 lawyers had been doing that work for
many, many years. I was certainly not aware of any issues or concerns - any issues that
would give me any cause for concern on the ethical or professional front. So I did not make it
a point to remind them of their ethical duties. They were professional litigators, and I felt
quite comfortable that they were following their ethical duties because I didn't see any
indication to the contrary. But it wasn't a thing that I raised or a tub that I thumped, to use
that term.
MR SCOTT: What level of supervision did you provide Mr Sparkes?
MR ROSER: I would say relatively minimal because he was a very senior and experienced
litigator who knew the law, and I was, as a General Counsel, in a more supervisory kind of
role. So I did not give any of my Deputy General Counsel or senior lawyers day - what you
might regard as day-to-day supervision.
COMMISSIONER: Just on that, knowing the law, this concept of best available evidence which
seems to pop up at every turn in DHS, where does it come from? What's the use of the best
available evidence if it's not probative?
MR ROSER: I can't tell you, Commissioner, about the genesis of the term, but I think my
simplistic view would be the best available evidence is the most probative evidence.
COMMISSIONER: But what if it actually does not prove the point you want to prove?
MR ROSER: Then you would regard it as something less than the best evidence,
Commissioner.
COMMISSIONER: But if that's all that's available, do you go ahead and use it?
MR ROSER: Yes.
COMMISSIONER: Even though it's not probative?
MR ROSER: It's a question of balance, perhaps, Commissioner, and the Briginshaw scale may
come into it, but I don't - - -
COMMISSIONER: Never mind Briginshaw.
MR ROSER: - - - want to get into that, Commissioner. But it would have to carry some
probative weight to able to be relied upon, of course.
COMMISSIONER: That's the point, you see.
MR ROSER: But there are questions of degree, and if other evidence is available but you still
have evidence that carries with it probative weight, then it's evidence upon which you can

COMMISSIONER: Yes. That's the qualification we never see. We just see "best available
evidence" with no regard to what it actually proves. Does it prove something?
MR ROSER: I can't speak for the genesis of the term in Human Services. That's my personal
approach to it.
COMMISSIONER: Thank you.
MR SCOTT: Thank you, Commissioner. Can I ask you this: have you ever come across any
judicial authority to the effect that it is an established principle of administrative law that an
administrative decision-maker is entitled to rely on the best available evidence even if it is
not probative of the issue?
MR ROSER: No, I have not.
MR SCOTT: Thank you. And that would be because no such principle exists?
MR ROSER: I would assume that to be the case. I don't know personally, I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Alright. That can be taken down. Now, Mr Roser, do you recall attending a
conference of the Australian Institute of Administrative Lawyers in July 2017?
MR ROSER: I certainly recall attending. I am afraid I don't recall the date, but I certainly recall
the conference.
MR SCOTT: Right. Did you watch Mr Hanks' presentation?
MR ROSER: Yes, I did.
MR SCOTT: Alright. Didn't he make clear in that presentation that an aspect of the Robodebt
Scheme was that it calculated and raised debts based on income averaging?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes, he did.
MR SCOTT: Right. And didn't he make it clear that, in his view, that was unlawful?
MR ROSER: Yes, he did.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Did that not cause you any concerns at that stage in July 2017?
MR ROSER: It did, to an extent. Yes.
MR SCOTT: I mean, you know who Mr Hanks is, of course, don't you?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes. I do.

MR SCOTT: Author of a - sorry, author of a textbook on constitutional law?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes.
MR SCOTT: An eminent silk?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Has appeared in the High Court?
MR ROSER: I would assume so. I - I can't be sure. I would assume so.
MR SCOTT: Has even been briefed to act on behalf of the Commonwealth in some matters as
well?
MR ROSER: Again, I would assume - I would assume that to be the case. I certainly wouldn't
be surprised if that were the case, but I don't know myself.
MR SCOTT: So you would agree that his opinion as to the lawfulness of the Scheme was
something to be taken seriously; correct?
MR ROSER: Correct.
MR SCOTT: And you recall also that he proposed in that conference that proceedings be
taken against the Commonwealth to test the lawfulness of the Robodebt Scheme?
MR ROSER: Yes, that's correct. He was effectively looking for the appropriate matter to bring
forward. That was quite clear.
MR SCOTT: Do you recall him saying to words to the effect they were hoping to get
something underway, that is, some proceedings underway in the next six months?
MR ROSER: I don't recall that specifically, but I certainly recall he was looking for that
appropriate matter to test.
MR SCOTT: Right.
MR ROSER: I don't recall the timing, I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So would you agree that at that stage it must have been apparent that the
Commonwealth faced potentially some very serious legal exposure?
MR ROSER: Yes.
MR SCOTT: Including reputational risk?

MR SCOTT: And indeed if his opinion were correct, that the Commonwealth was taking
money from social security recipients that it wasn't entitled to on a massive scale.
MR ROSER: If that - if that opinion proved to be correct, then that would also naturally flow,
yes.
MR SCOTT: So in light of what you heard and what you've just agreed with me on, what did
you do in terms of bringing those matters to the attention of the relevant people within the
Department of Human Services?
MR ROSER: Basically all of the relevant people that I would have spoken to about that issue
were at that conference and were as aware of the issue as I was. So there was no need for
me to make any further notifications that would - had already gone out.
MR SCOTT: Right. When you - did you speak to the people at the conference about the issue?
MR ROSER: Yes. Yes, I did. I spoke to my peers in the break after the - after Mr Hanks'
session, I recall.
MR SCOTT: Right. Could you give some names of who you spoke to?
MR ROSER: I think Maris Stipnieks was there. I - I recall Tim Ffrench might have been there as
well. Other people - I can't recall the specifics. Possibly Patrick Collins. Other people I can't
recall, I'm afraid.
MR SCOTT: And did they express any views to you on the issue?
MR ROSER: The views - the discussion was mainly around the fact that Mr Hanks was quite
expressly looking for a case to use as a test vehicle, for want of a better term, and that was
really the focus of the discussion.
MR SCOTT: After the conference, did you have a conversation with Annette Musolino about
the issue?
MR ROSER: Yes, we would have had - well, we did have many conversations about the issue,
as a general proposition, yes.
MR SCOTT: When?
MR ROSER: I couldn't recall specific instances, but it was a topic for discussion within the
Legal Services Division.
MR SCOTT: Did Ms Musolino express any words acknowledging the extent of the legal
exposure the Commonwealth potentially faced?

MR SCOTT: What words did she use?
MR ROSER: Well, I mean, there was a variety of discussions. I couldn't recall the content of
any particular one, but generally the discussions revolved around whether averaging was an
appropriate administrative decision-making basis for raising a debt.
MR SCOTT: Okay. So you don't recall at all any of the words that Ms Musolino used in these
discussions with you?
MR ROSER: Not the specific words, no.
MR SCOTT: Did you make it clear to her the extent of legal exposure you thought the
Commonwealth was faced with?
MR ROSER: I think we were all quite clear about the potential exposure and that it could be
significant is probably an understatement on a number of fronts. I didn't feel any need to
clarify that because I think it was known.
MR SCOTT: Did you express any views about whether or not an independent legal advice
should be obtained?
MR ROSER: No.
MR SCOTT: Okay. Did it occur to you that would have been a prudent course to adopt?
MR ROSER: No. No, I didn't think it was a prudent course to adopt at the time. No.
MR SCOTT: Why is that?
MR ROSER: This had been a decision and the Department had been operating the Scheme in
its various forms - I think it was originally OCI, and it might have had some changes in name
and changes in iterations - for some period of time. And if - if a legal test case was presented,
then that would surely be the time when advice was obtained.
MR SCOTT: Were you aware of any independent legal opinion on the lawfulness of averaging
as it was used in the Robodebt Scheme prior to the Masterton litigation?
MR ROSER: No. I'm not aware of any.
MR SCOTT: So, to be clear, an independent legal opinion obtained by the Commonwealth?
MR ROSER: I'm not aware of any.
MR SCOTT: Right. But you had, in effect, an independent legal opinion from an eminent
barrister in the form of Mr Hanks, didn't you?

MR ROSER: Well, I wouldn't call it necessarily an opinion, but it certainly - as in a set piece
legal opinion, but I think his view was clear that there were questions to be posed about the
Scheme, yes.
MR SCOTT: Would you agree with me this: that it was obvious from what he said at that
conference that if an independent legal opinion were obtained by the Department, there
was a substantial chance that opinion would confirm what Mr Hanks had said about the
unlawfulness of averaging in the Scheme?
MR ROSER: Well, certainly I think there would be a chance, but whether it would be
substantial - I - I couldn't have said at that time whether that was the appropriate sort of
term. Certainly a chance, yes, absolutely.
MR SCOTT: Well, you knew, didn't you, from the presentation by Mr Hanks in July 2017, that
averaging was being used to calculate and raise debts under the Scheme; correct?
MR ROSER: Correct.
MR SCOTT: And you knew from what Mr Hanks said that that was a process of averaging ATO
data; correct?
MR ROSER: Correct.
